monolithic system|monolithic kernel: The operating system operates as a single program in kernel mode, organized as a collection of procedures combined into a single executable; all OS components (process management, file system, drivers, memory management) operate within a single address space and share the same privilege level. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
main program|main procedure: A main program that invokes service procedures; like the "boss" of the system, it decides when and how to use different tools (services). See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
service procedures: A set of service procedures handling system calls; like tools in the toolbox, each one does a specific job, like reading a file, writing to disk, or managing memory. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
utility procedures: Utility procedures that support the service procedures; helper tools that don't interact with users directly, e.g. help with copying data or managing low-level details. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
loadable extension|kernel module: Besides the core OS, extensions (like device drivers or file systems) that are loaded on demand, such as shared libraries in Linux and DLLs in Windows. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
insmod: Inserting a module into the Linux Kernel. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
rmmod: Removing a module from the Linux Kernel. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
lsmod: Showing the status of modules in the Linux Kernel. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
dmesg: Printing the kernel ring buffer. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
layered system: The operating system is organized as a hierarchy of layers, each one constructed upon the one below it; each layer relies only on the one below it. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
THE system: The layered system built at the Technische Hogeschool Eindhoven in the Netherlands by E. W. Dijkstra (1968) and his students; layers 0 processor allocation and multiprogramming, 1 memory and drum management, 2 operator-process communication, 3 input/output management, 4 user programs, 5 the operator. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
MS-DOS (layered): Layers application program, resident system program, MS-DOS device drivers, ROM BIOS device drivers, where upper layers can also go straight to the ROM BIOS device drivers. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
microkernel: Splitting the operating system up into small, well-defined modules, only one of which—the microkernel—runs in kernel mode and the rest run as relatively powerless ordinary user processes; it minimizes the core kernel's responsibilities, running essential services (like inter-process communication and basic scheduling) within the kernel, while other services (like drivers and file systems) run in user space. See [Microkernels and the client-server model](#/comp4736-p2/microkernels-and-client-server).
MINIX 3: Microkernel example; the microkernel handles interrupts, processes, scheduling, IPC (with Clock and Sys in the kernel), while drivers, servers and user programs run in user mode. See [Microkernels and the client-server model](#/comp4736-p2/microkernels-and-client-server).
client-server model: Servers provide some service, clients use these services, communication between clients and servers is often by message passing; an abstraction that can be used for a single machine or for a network of machines. See [Microkernels and the client-server model](#/comp4736-p2/microkernels-and-client-server).
message passing: How clients and servers often communicate in the client-server model ("message from client to server"). See [Microkernels and the client-server model](#/comp4736-p2/microkernels-and-client-server).
virtualization: Allows you to run two or more operating systems using only one machine. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
shared hosting: (no virtualization) a login account on a Web server, but no control over the server software. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
dedicated hosting: (no virtualization) you have your own machine, very flexible but not cost effective. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
hypervisor|virtual machine monitor: "Hypervisor (virtual machine monitor)"; the layer under the guest operating systems in the type 1 / type 2 figure. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
type 1 hypervisor: Runs directly on system hardware, no need for an operating system (OS); example ESXi (Elastic Sky X Integrated). See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
type 2 hypervisor: Runs on a host operating system, guest OS on top; example VirtualBox with host OS Windows 10 and guest OS Tiny Core Linux. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
pure type 2 hypervisor: Figure (b): a machine simulator running on the host operating system with the guest OS on top. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
practical type 2 hypervisor: Figure (c): a type 2 hypervisor on the host operating system, with a kernel module in the host OS. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
host OS: The operating system the type 2 hypervisor runs on, e.g. Windows 10. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
guest OS: The operating system running inside a virtual machine, e.g. Tiny Core Linux. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
CP/CMS: Control Program/Cambridge Monitor System. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
CMS: CMS is a single user OS; runs on each virtual 370. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
VM/370: The VM-Virtualization Layer on 370 bare hardware that provides the virtual 370s; I/O instructions from CMS trap here. See [Virtual machines and hypervisors](#/comp4736-p2/virtual-machines).
exokernel: Listed (greyed out) as structure 6 on the agenda; not defined in the deck. See [Monolithic systems and layered systems](#/comp4736-p2/monolithic-and-layered).
crystal oscillator: Can generate a periodic signal, typically in the range of several hundred megahertz to a few gigahertz, depending on the crystal chosen. See [Clock hardware: crystal, counter, holding register](#/comp4736-p2/clock-hardware).
counter: The oscillator's signal is fed into the counter to make it count down to zero; when the counter gets to zero, it causes a CPU interrupt; the counter is decremented at each pulse. See [Clock hardware: crystal, counter, holding register](#/comp4736-p2/clock-hardware).
holding register: The value of the holding register is copied into the counter; used to load the counter. See [Clock hardware: crystal, counter, holding register](#/comp4736-p2/clock-hardware).
programmable clock: Its interrupt frequency can be controlled by software. See [Clock hardware: crystal, counter, holding register](#/comp4736-p2/clock-hardware).
one-shot mode: When the clock is started, it copies the value of the holding register into the counter and then decrements the counter at each pulse from the crystal; when the counter gets to zero, it causes an interrupt and stops until it is explicitly started again by the software. See [Clock hardware: crystal, counter, holding register](#/comp4736-p2/clock-hardware).
square-wave mode: After getting to zero it causes an interrupt, the value of the holding register is copied into the counter and whole process is repeated again indefinitely. See [Clock hardware: crystal, counter, holding register](#/comp4736-p2/clock-hardware).
clock tick: The periodic interrupts of square-wave mode. See [Clock hardware: crystal, counter, holding register](#/comp4736-p2/clock-hardware).
clock driver duties: Maintaining the time of day; preventing processes from running longer than allowed; accounting for CPU usage; handling alarm system call from user processes; providing watchdog timers for parts of system itself; profiling, monitoring, statistics gathering. See [The clock driver's duties: time of day, quantum, accounting](#/comp4736-p2/clock-software).
time of day in ticks: A tick counter of the time of day; at 60 Hz a 32-bit counter will overflow in just over 2 years; a 64-bit counter makes maintaining the counter more expensive since it has to be done many times a second. See [The clock driver's duties: time of day, quantum, accounting](#/comp4736-p2/clock-software).
time of day in seconds: The time of day is maintained in seconds, rather than in ticks, plus a count of ticks in the current second; a 32-bit count lasts ≈ 136 years. See [The clock driver's duties: time of day, quantum, accounting](#/comp4736-p2/clock-software).
boot-relative time: Count in ticks relative to the time the system was booted, rather than relative to a fixed external moment; current time = the stored time of day in the memory + counter. See [The clock driver's duties: time of day, quantum, accounting](#/comp4736-p2/clock-software).
quantum: The scheduler initializes a counter to the value of that process' quantum in clock ticks; at every clock interrupt the clock driver decrements it by 1, and at zero calls the scheduler to set up another process. See [The clock driver's duties: time of day, quantum, accounting](#/comp4736-p2/clock-software).
CPU usage accounting|second timer: A second timer, distinct from the main system timer, started whenever a process is started up and read out when it stops to tell how long the process has run; saved when an interrupt occurs and restored afterward. See [The clock driver's duties: time of day, quantum, accounting](#/comp4736-p2/clock-software).
alarm system call: A process can request that the operating system give it a warning (a signal, interrupt, message,…) after a certain interval. See [Alarm system calls, the next-signal list and watchdog timers](#/comp4736-p2/alarms-and-watchdogs).
simulating multiple timers|clock request: Simulate multiple clocks by chaining all the pending clock requests together, sorted on time, in a linked list; each entry tells how many clock ticks following the previous one to wait before causing a signal. See [Alarm system calls, the next-signal list and watchdog timers](#/comp4736-p2/alarms-and-watchdogs).
Next signal: The count decremented on each tick; when Next signal = 0 the signal for the first item on the list is caused and that item is removed. See [Alarm system calls, the next-signal list and watchdog timers](#/comp4736-p2/alarms-and-watchdogs).
watchdog timer: Detect and recover from crashes, infinite loops; a watchdog timer may reset a system that stops running, especially used in embedded system. See [Alarm system calls, the next-signal list and watchdog timers](#/comp4736-p2/alarms-and-watchdogs).
